title: The Hot Heart Under Your Feet

blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: Stamp your feet. Under your feet is the ground. Under the ground is rock. Under that rock is more rock, and it is warm. Go down and down and down. In the middle of the Earth is a big ball of iron. It glows. It is hotter than any fire you have ever seen. But you are safe. You are way up here, standing on the cool ground in your shoes.

blocks.prompt: The Earth Is Like a Peach
blocks.text: Cut a peach in half. It has thin skin on the outside. It has soft fruit in the middle. It has a hard pit right in the center. The Earth has layers like that. The top layer is the crust. The crust is the rock we walk on, and it is thin. Under the crust is the mantle. The mantle is hot rock. It moves, but it moves so slowly that you could never see it. Under the mantle is the core. The core is made of iron. The outside of the core is melted, like hot soup. The inside is a hard ball. It is the hottest place on Earth.

3.title: The Hot Heart Under Your Feet
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

notes: Four layers: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core
The crust is thinner than an eggshell, in proportion
The mantle creeps about as fast as your fingernails grow
The inner core is about as hot as the surface of the sun

blocks.prompt: Four Layers Down
blocks.text: The ground feels solid. It feels like it goes down forever. It does not. The rock you are standing on is a thin shell called the crust, and the Earth has three more layers under it. Under the crust is the mantle, and the mantle is enormous. It is hot rock, and it is not quite liquid and not quite still. It creeps. In a whole year, mantle rock might move as far as your fingernails grow. Under the mantle is the outer core. Here the iron is so hot that it has melted into a churning ocean of liquid metal. Right in the center is the inner core, another ball of iron. It is the hottest part of the Earth, about as hot as the surface of the sun. But it is not melted. It is squeezed so hard by everything above it that it stays solid. Nobody has ever been down there. The deepest hole people have ever drilled did not even get through the crust. It went about 7.6 miles down, and then the rock got too hot for the drill.

4.title: The Hot Heart Under Your Feet
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Hot Heart Under Your Feet

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: It is about 3,959 miles from the ground to the center
The mantle is about 84 percent of the Earth's volume
The deepest hole ever drilled: 7.6 miles, in Russia
That hole reached less than one fifth of one percent of the way down
The inner core is roughly 9,400 degrees Fahrenheit

blocks.prompt: The Deepest Hole We Ever Dug
blocks.text: From your shoes to the center of the Earth is about 3,959 miles. That is a long drive, and you would be driving through solid rock. So here is a fair question: if nobody has ever gone down there, how does anyone know what is down there at all? People did try digging. In 1970, scientists in the far north of Russia started drilling a hole for one reason only: to see how deep they could get. They kept at it for about twenty years. The Kola Superdeep Borehole finally reached 7.6 miles, which made it the deepest hole humans have ever made. Then they stopped, because the rock down there had turned out to be far hotter than anyone predicted, around 356 degrees Fahrenheit, and at that temperature the rock behaved less like stone and more like soft plastic. It kept squeezing the hole shut. Here is the humbling part. After twenty years of the hardest drilling ever attempted, that hole had traveled less than one fifth of one percent of the way to the center. It never even got through the crust. So drilling was never going to be the answer. What worked instead was listening. Every earthquake sends waves racing through the whole planet, and those waves bend, slow down, speed up, and bounce depending on what they pass through. Scientists set up instruments all over the world and read the waves as they arrive. The Earth rings, and we listen to the echo, and from that echo we draw the layers we will never see.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.

In your own words, explain how earthquake waves tell us what is inside the Earth.

answers: the rock was much hotter than expected and acted like soft plastic, squeezing the hole shut
twenty years of record drilling covered less than one fifth of one percent of the distance and never left the crust
(waves from earthquakes bend, slow, speed up, and bounce as they pass through different layers, and instruments read those changes)
(inference: waves reach the whole planet for free, while drills cannot survive the heat or the distance)

5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

meta.templateLabel: The Hot Heart Under Your Feet

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: P waves travel through solids and liquids; S waves only through solids
Richard Oldham, 1906: the core is liquid
Inge Lehmann, 1936: there is a solid core inside the liquid one
The S wave shadow zone covers about a third of the planet
Outer core: about 1,400 miles of churning liquid iron
Inner core: a solid iron ball about 760 miles across

blocks.prompt: The Woman Who Found the Inner Core
blocks.text: Nobody has ever seen inside the Earth. Everything we claim to know about the crust, the mantle, and the core was worked out from waves, and the waves came from earthquakes. Earthquakes release two useful kinds of wave. P waves push and pull the rock in the direction they travel, and they can move through anything, solid or liquid. S waves shake the rock sideways, and sideways shaking only works if the material can hold its shape. S waves travel through solids. They stop dead at liquid. In 1906, a British geologist named Richard Oldham noticed something strange in the records. After a large earthquake, there was a huge region on the far side of the planet where no S waves arrived at all. Instruments there sat quiet while stations elsewhere recorded the shaking. That silent region is now called the shadow zone, and it covers roughly a third of the globe. Oldham drew the only conclusion the evidence allowed. Something in the middle of the Earth was liquid, and it was swallowing the S waves. The Earth had a molten core. Thirty years later, a Danish seismologist named Inge Lehmann went back to the same shadow zone and found a flaw in the story. Faint P waves were arriving inside the zone, where the simple liquid core model said nothing should arrive. Lehmann worked through the arrival times by hand, with no computers, and proposed that the waves were bouncing off something. Inside the liquid outer core, she argued, sat a second core, and that one was solid. In 1936 she published the idea in a paper with one of the shortest titles in science: P'. She was right. The inner core is a ball of iron roughly 760 miles across, hotter than melted iron has any business being, kept solid by the crushing weight of three thousand miles of planet pressing down on it. Lehmann worked as a seismologist until she was past ninety. She never saw the thing she discovered. No one has. We know it is there because a wave came back when it should not have.

6.title: The Hot Heart Under Your Feet
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Hot Heart Under Your Feet

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Radius to the center: about 3,959 miles
Continental crust: roughly 25 miles thick; ocean crust: about 4
Mantle: about 1,800 miles of creeping solid rock
Outer core: liquid iron and nickel, the source of the magnetic field
Inner core: solid iron, near 9,400 degrees Fahrenheit
The inner core grows about a millimeter a year as the outer core freezes

blocks.prompt: The Engine We Have Never Seen
blocks.text: Consider how little of your own planet you have access to. From the soles of your shoes to the center of the Earth is about 3,959 miles. The deepest hole ever drilled reached 7.6 miles, and it took two decades of the most determined engineering anyone has attempted. That hole did not reach the mantle. It did not come close. Everything below the first few miles of rock is, in the most literal sense, unvisited. And yet we can describe it in detail, and the description is not a guess. The Earth is built in four layers, and they are less like the stripes on a diagram and more like a system doing work. The crust is the thin cold skin we live on, roughly 25 miles thick under the continents and only about 4 miles thick under the oceans. Beneath it lies the mantle, about 1,800 miles of rock that is technically solid and yet flows. Over millions of years, hot mantle rock rises, cools, and sinks in slow loops, and those loops drag the plates of the crust around with them. Continents move because the mantle is stirring. Beneath the mantle the material changes entirely. The outer core is liquid iron and nickel, a churning metal ocean about 1,400 miles deep. At the very center sits the inner core, a solid iron ball roughly 760 miles across at close to 9,400 degrees Fahrenheit, which is about the temperature of the surface of the sun. That should be far too hot to be solid, and it would be, at the surface. Down there the weight of the entire planet presses in from every direction, and the pressure locks the atoms in place. Heat wants to melt it; pressure will not let it. Now put those last two layers together, because they are the reason the surface is habitable. As the Earth slowly loses heat, the inner core grows, freezing outward by about a millimeter a year. That freezing stirs the liquid iron above it, and the planet's rotation twists the stirring into spirals. Moving liquid metal generates electric current, and electric current generates a magnetic field. The Earth is a dynamo. That field reaches far out into space, where it deflects the stream of charged particles the sun is constantly throwing at us, particles that would otherwise strip away the upper atmosphere over geological time. Every compass needle that swings north is reporting on a machine three thousand miles beneath it that no eye will ever inspect. So how do we know any of this? We listen. Every large earthquake sends waves through the entire body of the planet, and those waves refract, reflect, slow, and stop according to what they encounter. S waves cannot cross liquid, so the region where they fail to arrive maps the liquid core. P waves that arrive where no one expected them revealed the solid inner core to Inge Lehmann in 1936. The interior of the Earth was not discovered by going there. It was reconstructed, patiently and correctly, by people at the surface reading the echoes of the ground shaking under their feet.
